title: Twenty-Seven Body Parts to Apothecary Grains — How Language Built Number & Dosing

teenKit.tldr: Numbers aren't a universal law of the universe; they are a physical technology invented by humans using their own anatomy, evolving from body-part tracking into life-or-death ancient drug dosages.
teenKit.whyItMatters: Understanding that mathematics is a built tool rather than a cosmic abstraction reminds you that every single system of measurement you use today was engineered by humans to solve real survival problems.
keyTakeaways: Base-10 math isn't a cosmic inevitability, but a biological accident born entirely from having ten fingers.
Ancient cultures like the Oksapmin used a 27-locus body-counting system, mapping numbers directly across shoulders, elbows, wrists, and fingers.
As humanity moved from counting livestock to measuring toxic medical herbs, math evolved from simple tallying into a razor-thin boundary between life and fatal respiratory arrest.

quiz.question: Why do humans predominantly use a base-10 counting system today?
options: It is a hardcoded mathematical law of the universe.
It is a biological accident because primates happen to have ten fingers.
Ancient mathematicians discovered it was the only efficient way to calculate.
It was mandated by early global trade agreements.
quiz.explanation: Base-10 math is simply a byproduct of our primate anatomy having ten digits to count on.

quiz.question: How did the Oksapmin people of Papua New Guinea traditionally track numbers?
options: By tying knots in complex rope strings called quipus.
By carving tally marks into Paleolithic wolf bones.
By mapping numbers across a 27-locus sequence of body parts like wrists and elbows.
By using clay tokens sealed inside spherical envelopes.
quiz.explanation: The Oksapmin used a 27-body-part counting system where pointing to specific anatomical locations represented different quantitative values.

quiz.question: What high-stakes shift happened when ancient societies transitioned from basic tallying to apothecary metrology?
options: Math became a life-or-death boundary for measuring exact doses of toxic plant alkaloids.
Numbers became completely abstract and lost all connection to physical objects.
Governments stopped regulating weights and measures entirely.
Traders stopped using seeds as weight standards.
quiz.explanation: Weighing powerful botanical toxins required precise mathematical systems to avoid causing fatal overdoses.
